Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 259 columns across 4 data files.
#### Issues Identified

45 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: We thank Steven Pinker and Jeff Rosenberg for initial feedback on suitable domains and indicators.

Global governance runs on indicators, be it by governments to identify gaps and set goals, by international agencies to target and evaluate interventions, or by researchers to measure and track societal change.
Pragmatically, indicators must also reliably track change across populations to drive timely intervention in critical domains.

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were in part designed to address related shortcomings in the Millennium Development Goals, expanding from 48 to 233 indicators co-selected by national and international agencies, to measure change more precisely [1, 2].
text.formatted: The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were in part designed to address related shortcomings in the Millennium Development Goals, expanding from 48 to 233 indicators co-selected by national and international agencies, to measure change more precisely <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: However, it remains an open question if public measures of progress (such as the SDGs) meet the minimum criteria needed before their validity can even be assessed: whether they can be inspected, whether data exists, and if this data is kept current to track the world's most pressing challenges.
Here, we aim to start filling this gap.
Assessing whether an indicator tracks change validly depends on two prerequisites: how it is conceived, and the data it relies on.
First, an indicator may inadequately capture the theoretical construct it claims to measure.
Gross domestic product (GDP), for instance, is often treated as a holistic marker of progress despite its narrow scope and warnings by critics and its own architect [3, 4].
text.formatted: Gross domestic product (GDP), for instance, is often treated as a holistic marker of progress despite its narrow scope and warnings by critics and its own architect <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, early versions of the Human Development Index were constructed to replace the GDP's misuse by capturing broader dimensions of human well-being (e.g., longevity, education, income; [5].
text.formatted: Similarly, early versions of the Human Development Index were constructed to replace the GDP's misuse by capturing broader dimensions of human well-being (e.g., longevity, education, income; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Yet aggregation of distinct dimensions into a single index obscured the relations between them by weighting them equally.

To assess an indicator's validity, social science methodologists have long advocated for the conceptual clarity guided by adequate quantification and transparent documentation on how indicators are composed or estimated [6, 7].
text.formatted: To assess an indicator's validity, social science methodologists have long advocated for the conceptual clarity guided by adequate quantification and transparent documentation on how indicators are composed or estimated <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Yet such debates presuppose that an indicator is defined, documented, and publicly available; whether commonly used indicators meet even these prerequisites is rarely examined.
Second, a well-constructed indicator cannot reliably measure global progress if its data is incomplete or too sparse.

How is one to assess the validity of SDG indicators when country coverage varies from 80% for clean energy to under 20% for climate action, with nearly a third of indicators not updated in the last few years [8]?
text.formatted: How is one to assess the validity of SDG indicators when country coverage varies from 80% for clean energy to under 20% for climate action, with nearly a third of indicators not updated in the last few years <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>?

text.text: These concerns are not necessarily novel nor unique to global governance.
Consider the flawed demographic projections of runaway population growth in China, which provided the technical justification for the disastrous one-child policy [9].
text.formatted: Consider the flawed demographic projections of runaway population growth in China, which provided the technical justification for the disastrous one-child policy <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Or consider how modern public and private sectors alike often rely on inadequately specified sustainability targets and poorly operationalized performance metrics, constraining program efforts [10].
text.formatted: Or consider how modern public and private sectors alike often rely on inadequately specified sustainability targets and poorly operationalized performance metrics, constraining program efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Others have discussed how weak national statistical systems [8] and administrative decisions to curtail data infrastructures may undermine assessment of the validity for global progress indicators [e.g., 11-13].
text.formatted: Others have discussed how weak national statistical systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> and administrative decisions to curtail data infrastructures may undermine assessment of the validity for global progress indicators [e.g., 11-13].

text.text: However, these common critiques have chiefly focused on single indicators or issues [e.g., [14] [15] [16], leaving open how a broad set of commonly used indicators perform against the basic prerequisites outlined above.
text.formatted: However, these common critiques have chiefly focused on single indicators or issues [e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, leaving open how a broad set of commonly used indicators perform against the basic prerequisites outlined above.

text.text: Several existing frameworks have attempted to address these prerequisites.
For instance, the OECD/JRC Handbook [17] addresses the construction of composite indices, including metadata, comparability and robustness.
text.formatted: For instance, the OECD/JRC Handbook <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> addresses the construction of composite indices, including metadata, comparability and robustness.

text.text: In turn, the FAIR principles [18] concern data infrastructure standards, and the Cape Town Global Action Plan [19] has addressed gaps in national statistical systems.
text.formatted: In turn, the FAIR principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> concern data infrastructure standards, and the Cape Town Global Action Plan <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> has addressed gaps in national statistical systems.

text.text: Finally, European Statistical System (ESS) and IMF frameworks , 21] set comprehensive quality criteria largely for their own assessment (which may preclude valid global comparisons of indicators), whereas IAEG-SDG tier system [2] grades SDG indicators on methodological maturity and data availability.
text.formatted: Finally, European Statistical System (ESS) and IMF frameworks , 21] set comprehensive quality criteria largely for their own assessment (which may preclude valid global comparisons of indicators), whereas IAEG-SDG tier system <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> grades SDG indicators on methodological maturity and data availability.

text.text: Because each of these frameworks addresses only part of the problem, we sought to adapt their central principles into a compact audit framework to assess whether indicators meet minimum criteria to assess validity as global measures of progress (see Table 1).
text.formatted: Because each of these frameworks addresses only part of the problem, we sought to adapt their central principles into a compact audit framework to assess whether indicators meet minimum criteria to assess validity as global measures of progress (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Drawing from publicly accessible data, scoring each criterion separable, and applying the same rules to heterogenous produces allows informative yet quick comparison across diverse sets of indicators.

From the aims and principles of existing frameworks, we have derived six prerequisites to address issues in assessing indicator validity: definability, quantifiability, public data availability, population coverage, documentation and annual updating.
First, the construct must be definable, so that everyone is talking about the same phenomenon and the indicator can be quantifiable, with specified units and procedures.
Data must be available in practice, since specified procedures are only as useful as the numbers they produce.

An indicator aspiring to measure humanity's progress ought to adequately sample from at least half the world's population (similar to the IAEG's criterion, [2]) so that conclusions about "global progress" do not simply reflect the experience of a handful of nations.
text.formatted: An indicator aspiring to measure humanity's progress ought to adequately sample from at least half the world's population (similar to the IAEG's criterion, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>) so that conclusions about "global progress" do not simply reflect the experience of a handful of nations.

text.text: Documentation must be transparent, so that independent analysts can audit estimation methods and understand indicator composition.

Finally, indicators require temporal resolution of at least annual updates within the last decade (since indicator coding in 2024), providing a feedback loop policymakers can use to detect emerging risks or verify whether an intervention is working.

This threshold follows from the monitoring purpose rather than from measurement quality per se: an indicator updated every five years cannot register a shock, or a response to it, until long after decisions have been made.
We consider these criteria to be minimal but necessary requirements for beginning to evaluate whether an indicator may be a valid measure of global progress.
To evaluate our audit's utility, we applied the framework to 99 candidate indicators spanning eight domains of progress and six additional domains proposed by leading field experts.

We assembled them from two sources: 62 nominated by 24 experts primarily from social and economic sciences, augmented by 37 indicators pre-selected by the research team based on common policy and research use.

Two coders independently identified the best online data source for each indicator, scoring definability, quantifiability, and data availability sequentially before assessing the remaining data-level criteria in parallel.

In doing so, the audit extends to societal indicators the scrutiny recently directed at validity and measurement practice within psychology [22], and provides an openly available, reusable assessment of the metrics on which claims about human progress rest.

text.text: Though these domains may not reflect the full breadth of human welfare, we chose them because they capture a large range of concerns relevant to societal well-being and progress.
Critically, experts had the opportunity to suggest indicators for domains outside this breadth.
Indicators were assessed on meeting a set of minimum criteria necessary (but not sufficient) for valid measurement of societal change.
Two team members (MM, PD) each independently identified the best available online data source from their search and evaluated the indicator and dataset on the following criteria: 1.
Definability-i.e., the indicator can be precisely and concretely specified; 2.
Quantifiability-i.e., the indicator can be measured by number, degree, or presence of specific events; 3.
Publicly available data-i.e., indicator data were available online and accessible for evaluation.

We required that all "pre-selected indicators" satisfied up to this criterion as these indicators also served as items in a separate expert surveyfoot_1 (see Supplemental Methods) for a broader, parent study [30]; 4.
text.formatted: We required that all "pre-selected indicators" satisfied up to this criterion as these indicators also served as items in a separate expert survey<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> (see Supplemental Methods) for a broader, parent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>; 4.

text.text: Global population coverage-i.e., sampled countries reflected at least half of the global population in any year in the last decade.
Indicators that represented a global metric (e.g., "size of smallest chips in mass production") were treated as automatically passing this criterion; 5.
Publicly accessible documentation, based on indicators passing both following subcriteria: i.
Data documentation-i.e., accessible metadata explained data aggregation, missing data estimation, and extrapolation methods to explain data from the last decade; j.

Composition documentation-i.e., accessible metadata explained the composition and relational structure of sub-indicators within composite indicators (i.e., indicators that do not exist as real-world phenomena but are an index of multiple other markers, e.g., socioeconomic status may be derived from income, education, wealth, etc., but cannot be directly measured).
Direct indicators (e.g., "crude birth rate") were treated as passing this criterion automatically; 6.
Temporal resolution-i.e., data are systematically updated on a yearly basis for the last ten years since 2024, such as from data collection and/or extrapolation.
Team members (MM, PD) first assessed whether the indicator alone met definable and quantifiable criteria.
If indicators passed these criteria, data sources were assessed along with the remaining criteria.
As pre-selected indicators were required to meet up to "publicly available data" to be used as a survey item, these indicators were only evaluated based on their dataset.
For expert-recommended indicators, data sources used for assessment were either sources explicitly the influence of these biases is arguably limited.
suggested in experts' responses 3 , or, if no data sources were suggested, were separately identified by each team member from online sources.

text.text: This included indicators for new domains suggested by experts.
After independent coding of data sources, team members reconvened to discuss final selection and scoring of indicators.
If identified data sources differed between team members, the most representative and highest scoring data source was used to represent the indicator in the final score.

Overall indicator quality was scored sequentially for the first three criteria (definable, quantifiable, publicly available data), given quantification necessitated indicators to be defined, and available data necessitated quantification.
If initial criteria were met, remaining criteria (global population coverage, publicly accessible documentation, temporal resolution) were evaluated and scored non-sequentially.
For example, if an indicator met the definable and quantifiable criteria but lacked data, it would only be scored to quantifiable and none of the remaining criteria would be evaluated.
If an indicator met all three initial criteria but only met "temporal resolution," it was scored as meeting four of the six criteria.
Scores therefore reflect how far an indicator progressed through the audit, and not how many criteria it would satisfy if each were assessed independently.

We evaluated 99 indicators from pre-selection (n = 37, see Table S3) and expert suggestions (n = 62, see Table S2) in the eight pre-selected domains of civil liberties (n = 5), climate (n = 17), economy (n = 14), education (n = 4), mental health and happiness (n = 3), peace and war (n = 14), public health (n = 18), and technology (n = 16) with the remaining indicators belonging to expert-suggested domains.

text.text: Some failed at the level of scope: for instance, it is unclear what an indicator of the "weakening of public policies" would include, since it does not specify which policies count as public.
Others failed at the level of construct: an indicator of "existential risk" offers no operational way to distinguish an existential risk from one that is merely severe or catastrophic.
Of the 87 definable and quantifiable indicators across datasets, 12 (13.8%) lacked any existing, or publicly accessible, data.
Some of these could not be measured with current methods; for example, there is no commonly-agreed methodology for attributing deaths to climate change.
Others could not be audited because the data were not publicly accessible (e.g., official counts of weapons of mass destruction, including biological and chemical weapons, as classified by states).

Of the remaining 75 indicators, four (5.3%) only met the core criteria but none of the remaining criteria, failing criteria for global population coverage, sufficient documentation, and temporal resolution of data.
Following assessment of indicators against initial criteria, 25.4% of n = 71 remaining indicators) met only the global population coverage criterion beyond the initial criteria.

Their data span at least half the world's population, but they provided neither annual estimates for timely intervention nor sufficient documentation of how values were aggregated, estimated, or extrapolated or, for composite indicators, how scores were composed.
"Robot density" and "cold stress and hot stress" indicators also met four criteria, but only meeting temporal resolution and documentation criteria, respectively.
The remaining 49 indicators met at least five criteria, though nine of them (18.4%) still failed one or both documentation sub-criteria.

Another nine were adequately documented and had sufficient global coverage but were not updated annually, and one indicator ("overdose deaths") met documentation and temporal resolution data but failed to capture the global populace.
Overall, only 32 of the 99 societal indicators (32.3%, including indicators from expertsuggested domains) met all six criteria.
Of all candidates with available data (i.e., meeting initial criteria, n = 75), only 42.7% of indicators met all remaining criteria.
We found no reliable differences in indicator quality across domains (Figure 2).

Most domains appeared at both the lower and upper ends of the distribution, and no domain dominated the indicators meeting all criteria.

Questions about how to track societal progress are central to concerns about the present and the future.

Despite concerted efforts by individual nations and the global community to understand the direction of societal progress, our systematic audit reveals that fewer than onethird of 99 expert-nominated or commonly-used indicators satisfy the six basic prerequisites for assessing measurement validity.
Indicators that did meet these criteria appear to share institutional and methodological advantages.
Many originate from long-established institutions (e.g., NASA, NOAA, IMF) with existing mandates for standardization, transparency, and cross-national comparability.
Metrics from these organizations also reflect clearly defined, quantifiable constructs with welldocumented procedures.
Many also draw on near-continuous monitoring systems with extensive global coverage.

Even political indicators from Freedom House and V-Dem Institute benefit from standardized definitions and annual updates covering most states, suggesting even more "human" and holistic markers may achieve the same rigor.
Perhaps most importantly, documentation and temporal resolution criteria appeared as major bottlenecks in indicator success in our audit.

Institutions such as NASA, the World Bank, and Freedom House routinely publish open-access data, metadata, and methodological documentation, necessary for open critique, targeted usage for intervention, or replication.

Though temporal resolution may be more difficult to achieve, given resources and time, a measure of progress must consistently track temporal change, which may be achieved from routine data collection and/or sound estimate extrapolation.
Assessing the validity of these timepoints in turn requires freely accessible documentation, so that anyone can evaluate an indicator's methods and composition.
The audit points to concrete improvements that producers and funders can make to improve indicators.

Given most failures appeared for documentation and temporal resolution criteria, the most direct improvements producers can make are providing more accessible methods documentation (in estimation and composition) and improving update schedules to capture trends from noise [31, 32].
text.formatted: Given most failures appeared for documentation and temporal resolution criteria, the most direct improvements producers can make are providing more accessible methods documentation (in estimation and composition) and improving update schedules to capture trends from noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, clearer definitions, population coverage reporting, and source-selection rules may reduce failures of the other criteria.
These requirements could be checked routinely against public materials, as in our audit.
Where an indicator claims to predict future outcomes, it could also be tested against simple forecasting baselines.
Descriptive indicators call for different evidence, such as agreement with reference measurements, consistency across sources, or sensitivity to meaningful change.
Beyond these steps, we offer two more speculative recommendations.

Given political interference [11] [12] [13], an independent body could register indicator protocols in advance and publish periodic scorecards against criteria like ours, which may matter most for indicators controlled by private firms with little incentive to disclose their methods.
text.formatted: Given political interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, an independent body could register indicator protocols in advance and publish periodic scorecards against criteria like ours, which may matter most for indicators controlled by private firms with little incentive to disclose their methods.

text.text: To improve data production, emerging big data sources, such as satellite imagery, administrative data partnerships, and low-cost sensor networks, may also extend coverage where traditional surveys are infrequent, such as nations with weak national statistical systems.

Open-data licenses and version-controlled repositories attached to funding for such sources would lock transparency into the infrastructure, allowing at-will data auditing and discouraging retreating from this system.
However, such systems necessitate intergovernmental commitments to long-term maintenance to ensure systematic temporal resolution of critical societal phenomena.

It is possible that our team, dominated by psychologists and forecasting scientists, may have lacked the specialized expertise and knowledge needed to access and evaluate some technical indicators fully.
If so, the audit may underestimate the share of indicators that meet our criteria; conversely, retaining the higher-scoring data source when coders disagreed may have inflated it.
Future research and audit evaluations should directly engage with domain-specific experts to refine these evaluations further and move toward direct assessment of indicator validity.

We deliberately set the temporal threshold at annual updating because our audit asked whether indicators could support timely responses to societal challenges and shocks; by this standard, a series updated every three to five years would arrive too late to inform action, however well it would be measuring its construct.

Some indicators that failed this criterion, particularly for slow-moving constructs such as educational attainment or values measured in periodic surveys, may therefore be adequate for describing long-run change but inadequate for rapid response.
Conversely, update frequency is not the only barrier to timeliness: an annually updated series published several years after its reference period offers little more feedback than a five-yearly one.
Because we did not assess publication lag, the audit may overstate the share of indicators that can support rapid response.
Another caveat concerns the effort expert participants devoted to nominating domains and indicators.

Greater deliberation might have produced more reliable suggestions, but it is unclear whether additional time would have reduced bias (systematic differences such as favouring climate over economic indicators due to one's political ideology) or merely noise (random variability in judgments; [33]).
text.formatted: Greater deliberation might have produced more reliable suggestions, but it is unclear whether additional time would have reduced bias (systematic differences such as favouring climate over economic indicators due to one's political ideology) or merely noise (random variability in judgments; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>).

text.text: Noise can also originate in the indicators themselves when the societal phenomena they track fluctuate in ways that current instruments cannot capture.
In an era where data integrity is increasingly threatened by political pressures and misrepresentation, transparent, rigorous, and globally inclusive measurement frameworks become indispensable.
Only by building on that foundation can progress indicators move from pundits' talking points to trustworthy guides for human welfare.
